screens.title: Data Models and APIs for Network Devices
screens.narratorSegment: In modern networking we move from typing commands to telling devices what state we want. This lesson explains the two cooperating pieces that make programmatic networking reliable: data models and APIs. A data model, specifically YANG, is the schema or blueprint that describes what configuration and state look like. An A P I like NETCONF or RESTCONF is the channel we use to read and change that data. You will learn why a common model matters, how NETCONF uses XML and RPCs over a secure transport with transactional operations, and how RESTCONF maps YANG to familiar HTTP methods and JSON payloads. We include practical examples you can run with curl and show the precise structure you must use so your scripts are robust across vendors and device versions. By the end you'll understand not only the vocabulary but how to choose the right tool for tasks, how to avoid common mistakes like wrong namespaces or inadequate privileges, and how to test safely in a lab before touching production devices. Imagine YANG as the blueprint of a house: it defines rooms, wiring and constraints. The APIs are your construction crew — one follows rigid contracts and transactions, the other speaks web-native HTTP. Which crew you pick depends on the work and risk: we'll make that decision easier.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives target practical skills you need for safe, repeatable network automation. First, you'll explain why data models like YANG are necessary: they define the shape, types and constraints of configuration so automation tools interpret device data consistently. Second, you'll differentiate NETCONF and RESTCONF by their transport, encoding and operational model so you can choose the right A P I for a task. Third, you'll describe NETCONF and RESTCONF operations in detail, including NETCONF RPCs and RESTCONF HTTP methods, and how datastores and namespaces affect calls. Fourth, you'll demonstrate basic interactions using curl or a Python requests example to retrieve or change a hostname, showing exactly how to format requests and what to expect from the device. Each objective includes examples and a verification milestone so you can test competency in a lab. Achieving these objectives will let you automate deterministic changes, recover from mistakes, and integrate device APIs into higher-level automation tools. A frequent misconception is that APIs remove the need to understand the device model; in fact, model literacy is essential for correct paths, namespaces, and safe changes. We'll emphasize verification, minimal privileges and lab testing throughout.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Targets
screens.narratorSegment: These practice targets guide your lab work and assessments. First, identify the correct YANG path and namespace for a configuration element and explain how the model constrains valid values. For example, find the YANG path for an interface address or hostname and note required children. Second, map NETCONF RPCs to the state change you want: when to use edit-config and commit, when to lock a datastore, and why get-config differs from get. Third, write and run curl commands that authenticate to a RESTCONF endpoint, request JSON responses, and interpret the output. Fourth, adopt safety practices: use lab devices, minimize privileges, prefer idempotent HTTP methods, and confirm changes with a read-back. Each objective pairs a small verification: a GET that shows expected JSON, an edit that succeeds or rolls back, and a short explanation of the chosen path. These targets reduce accidental outages by making your automation predictable and verifiable before deployment. Remember, tools help, but model literacy and careful testing make automation safe.

screens.title: Data Models vs APIs: What each does
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a precise distinction: a data model defines what data looks like and what rules apply; an A P I defines how you ask for or change that data. YANG is a data modeling language that describes configuration nodes, types, constraints and relationships. It specifies that an interface object, for example, includes fields such as description, IP address and operational status. Without such a model, a script might try different field names depending on the device, which breaks automation. APIs are the transport and syntax you use to interact with those modeled elements. NETCONF provides an XML-based RPC mechanism over a secure transport, with built-in operations like get, get-config, edit-config, commit and lock. RESTCONF exposes YANG-modeled data as HTTP resources, letting you use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with JSON or XML payloads. A useful analogy: YANG is an architectural blueprint, and NETCONF or RESTCONF are contractors who read that blueprint and execute changes. A common misconception is to assume that choosing an A P I removes the need to understand the model; in reality, correct A P I usage depends on knowing the exact YANG paths and namespaces. Practically, this means before running automation you must inspect the device's YANG modules, confirm namespaces and test read operations. The takeaway is simple: learn the model, then use the A P I. Which leads to safer, repeatable automation.

keyIdea.title: Definition summary
keyIdea.text: YANG describes the data; NETCONF and RESTCONF provide the methods to read and change that data reliably.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Data Models vs APIs
What a data model does
YANG defines nodes, types, constraints and relationships so tools can parse and validate device data. It is the canonical schema that automation uses to find and set values.
Structured schema
Hierarchical paths and types prevent ambiguous field names.
Validation
Constraints ensure values follow expectations, reducing runtime errors.
Vendor openness
Common models let multi-vendor automation succeed.
What an API does
NETCONF and RESTCONF provide the protocol, encoding and operations to read and manipulate YANG-modeled data. The API enforces how requests and replies are framed and transported.
NETCONF
XML RPCs, SSH transport, transactional edits and datastore locking.
RESTCONF
HTTP methods, URIs mapped to YANG paths, JSON payloads and HTTPS transport.
Example
A YANG model defines that hostname exists under native/hostname. RESTCONF will expose that as a URI you can GET or PATCH.
Misconception
Think API alone is enough. In practice you must read the model to construct correct calls.
Takeaway
Model first, API second. That ordering reduces brittle automation.

screens.title: YANG: Structure and purpose
screens.narratorSegment: YANG is a language for expressing the schema of configuration and operational data on network devices. It defines containers, lists, leaf nodes, types and constraints so every element has a clear meaning. For example, a YANG model can require that an interface leaf supports an IP address with a specific pattern, or that a hostname leaf is a string under the native container. These definitions help automation by making values predictable and validating inputs before they're applied. A useful practice is to inspect the device's published YANG modules to find the correct namespace and hierarchical path; this step avoids the common error of referencing the wrong model or prefix. YANG also defines RPCs and notifications for device-specific operations and events, so you can standardize not only static configuration but also actions and alerts. A common misconception is that YANG is only for vendors; in reality it is an industry standard, and many vendors publish models for features across IOS XE and NX-OS. Practically, reading a YANG model is like reading a schema: it tells you what fields exist, which are mandatory, and the correct types. That knowledge is essential before crafting NETCONF XML or RESTCONF JSON payloads. Ask yourself: before you automate, have you opened the model and confirmed the exact path and namespace you will use?

keyIdea.title: YANG takeaway
keyIdea.text: Inspect and understand the YANG model for any element you plan to automate so your calls use correct paths and types.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › YANG Structure
YANG building blocks
  • Container — groups related nodes, like native features under a common parent.
  • List — repeated entries, such as interfaces or VLANs identified by a key.
  • Leaf — a single value node, for example hostname or IP address.
  • Types & constraints — enforce expected formats and ranges to reduce invalid inputs.
Tip: Always check the module's namespace and path before forming API calls.
Practical inspection
Devices often expose YANG modules via a developer portal or through the device itself. Locate the module that contains the element you need and note mandatory children and default values.
Concrete example
If a model requires hostname inside Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native, your RESTCONF URI must include that exact module name to retrieve or update the field.
Misconception
YANG is optional. In truth, it's the canonical way automation understands device structure.
Why it matters
Correct models prevent invalid writes and make multi-vendor automation feasible.
Check
Have you confirmed the namespace and mandatory leaves before your first API call?

screens.title: NETCONF fundamentals and standard operations
screens.narratorSegment: NETCONF is an XML-based management protocol designed for network configuration. It operates over a secure transport, typically SSH, and uses remote procedure calls to request actions. Core operations include get to retrieve running configuration and state, get-config to fetch a specific datastore like running or startup, edit-config to propose changes to a target datastore, and commit to apply candidate changes to running. NETCONF supports a candidate datastore model where you stage changes and then commit them atomically, which reduces the risk of partial updates. Lock and unlock are important when concurrent actors may modify the same datastore; you lock to prevent others from changing it during your session. NETCONF replies are XML-encoded and include detailed status information. A concrete example: you assemble an XML edit-config payload that includes the native hostname element from the device's YANG module, send the RPC, then inspect the rpc-reply for success. A common misconception is that NETCONF is only for reads; in fact it was built specifically to make reliable configuration changes with transactional guarantees. The practical takeaway is to use NETCONF when you need atomic edits and explicit locking, especially in multi-user or multi-tool environments where consistency matters most.

keyIdea.title: NETCONF core
keyIdea.text: Use NETCONF for transactional, atomic edits and strong datastore control with XML RPCs over SSH.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › NETCONF Fundamentals
Standard NETCONF operations
get — retrieve running configuration and state data.
get-config — fetch a specific datastore such as running or startup.
edit-config — stage configuration changes to a target datastore.
commit — apply staged changes atomically to running.
lock / unlock — prevent concurrent modifications while you operate.
Why choose NETCONF?
NETCONF is ideal when you need transactions, consistent commits, and explicit locking in multi-user environments.
Key Takeaway

NETCONF gives you robust configuration control through RPCs, datastores and transactional commits.

screens.title: NETCONF example: XML edit-config
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete NETCONF RPC payload used to set a hostname. NETCONF uses XML-encoded RPCs that include namespaces to identify the YANG module holding the target element. In this pattern you send an edit-config RPC that targets the running datastore and contains a config element with the module-qualified native container and the hostname leaf. The device responds with an rpc-reply indicating success or failure. Key details to note are the message-id for tracking, the base NETCONF namespace, and the module namespace for the specific element. A common mistake is omitting the module namespace or using an incorrect prefix; that causes the device to ignore the element or return an error. After sending the RPC, always inspect rpc-reply for ok or error details and consider using lock and commit when multiple processes might modify the datastore. The takeaway: constructing XML with the correct namespaces and using NETCONF's transactional semantics gives predictable, atomic configuration changes. Practice by comparing the payload to the device's YANG module so you confirm exact element names and structure. NETCONF example: XML edit-config means xml must include the correct netconf and module namespaces; missing or wrong namespaces lead to ignored or rejected edits.. In practical terms, a runnable xml rpc to set a hostname. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: XML must include the correct NETCONF and module namespaces; missing or wrong namespaces lead to ignored or rejected edits.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › NETCONF edit-config
Example XML payload
<rpc message-id="101" xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0"> <edit-config> <target> <running/> </target> <config> <native xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-native"> <hostname>MyAutomatedRouter</hostname> </native> </config> </edit-config> </rpc>
Annotations
  • xmlns — identifies the NETCONF base namespace on the rpc element.
  • native xmlns — module namespace for hostname; must match device YANG module.
  • message-id — correlates request and rpc-reply for tracking.
  • target — selects the datastore you are editing, e.g., running or candidate.
Common mistake: wrong module URI or omitted namespace; the payload may be accepted but ignored or rejected.

screens.title: NETCONF transactional behavior and locking
screens.narratorSegment: NETCONF includes mechanisms to make configuration changes safe and consistent. The typical workflow uses a candidate datastore: the client sends edits to the candidate, validates them, and then issues a commit to apply all changes to the running datastore in one atomic operation. If validation fails or an error occurs, you can discard the candidate, preventing partial updates. Lock and unlock protect a datastore from concurrent changes by other clients; use them when multiple automation tools or engineers might modify the same area. This transactional model prevents race conditions that occur when two processes try to update the same interface or route at the same time. A practical example: lock the running datastore, send a series of edit-config RPCs to update interface descriptions and IP addresses, validate the candidate, then commit. If any step fails, call discard-changes or unlock and investigate. A common misconception is that commits are instantaneous and risk-free; commits can fail due to validation, resource limits, or vendor-specific constraints, so always check rpc-reply details and plan rollback procedures. The key takeaway: use candidate + commit and lock/unlock to ensure predictable, all-or-nothing configuration changes under NETCONF.

keyIdea.title: Transactional control
keyIdea.text: Use candidate datastores and locking so configuration changes are atomic and protected from concurrent modification.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › NETCONF Transactions
Workflow
  1. Lock the datastore you will change to prevent concurrent edits.
  2. Send edit-config RPCs to a candidate or target datastore.
  3. Validate the candidate configuration and resolve errors.
  4. Commit the candidate to running as an atomic operation.
  5. Unlock the datastore when completed.
This sequence ensures either all changes apply or none do, avoiding partial states that can lead to network instability.
Quick checks
  • Always inspect rpc-reply for ok or errors.
  • Plan rollback if commit fails due to validation or resources.
  • Prefer candidate + commit for multi-step changes.
Pitfall: omitting a lock in a multi-client environment can lead to race conditions and conflicting edits.

screens.title: RESTCONF overview and HTTP method mapping
screens.narratorSegment: RESTCONF is an HTTP-based protocol that maps YANG-modeled data to RESTful resources. It typically operates over HTTPS and uses JSON or XML payloads. The mapping is straightforward: YANG containers and lists become hierarchical URIs, and standard HTTP methods correspond to operations on those resources. Use GET to retrieve configuration or operational data, POST to create new entries, PUT to replace a resource, PATCH to partially update, and DELETE to remove a resource. RESTCONF commonly returns JSON when you request application/yang-data+json. Because RESTCONF uses familiar web concepts, it is often easier for web developers and microservices to integrate with network devices. A common misconception is that RESTCONF is always less reliable than NETCONF; while it is more web-native and lightweight, RESTCONF still relies on YANG for structure and can be used safely if you understand idempotency semantics of methods like PUT and PATCH. Use RESTCONF when you prefer HTTP ecosystems, integration with web tooling, or lightweight JSON payloads. For transactional guarantees, consider whether your workflow requires NETCONF's explicit commit semantics, because RESTCONF typically relies on HTTP's idempotency rather than multi-step commits.

keyIdea.title: RESTCONF core
keyIdea.text: RESTCONF exposes YANG data via URIs and HTTP methods; pick it for web-native, JSON-friendly automation but be mindful of idempotency differences.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › RESTCONF Mapping
HTTP method mapping
  • GET — retrieve configuration or operational data.
  • POST — create a new resource, such as a new VLAN entry.
  • PUT — replace an existing resource or create if absent.
  • PATCH — partially update an existing resource.
  • DELETE — remove a resource.
URIs and encoding
URI paths include module-qualified containers, for example /restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/hostname. Use Accept and Content-Type headers with application/yang-data+json for JSON encoding.
Practical note: RESTCONF is easy to integrate with web tooling, but verify idempotency when choosing PUT vs PATCH.
Example URI
/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/hostname returns the hostname attribute in JSON.
Misconception
RESTCONF is not automatically transactional; rely on idempotent methods and read-back verification.
Check
Does your integration need atomic multi-step commits? If so, evaluate NETCONF instead.

screens.title: RESTCONF curl examples: GET and PATCH
screens.narratorSegment: We'll step through two practical curl examples you can run in a lab with RESTCONF enabled. The first retrieves the device hostname using an HTTP GET and requests JSON encoding. Note the Accept header set to application/yang-data+json and use of basic authentication for simplicity in a test environment. The second example uses PATCH to partially update the native container and change the hostname. In both commands replace placeholders with your device IP and credentials, and avoid using insecure flags in production. After PATCH, verify the change by performing the GET again or logging into the CLI. A common mistake is to forget the module prefix in the URI or to omit the Content-Type header for JSON payloads, causing the device to reject or ignore the change. screens.title: NETCONF vs RESTCONF — When to use each
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between NETCONF and RESTCONF depends on the task and environment. NETCONF offers strong transactional semantics, explicit locking, and XML RPCs tailored for configuration management; it is ideal when you need atomic multi-step changes or when multiple tools may concurrently update the same datastore. RESTCONF uses HTTP methods and JSON or XML payloads and maps YANG to URIs, making it convenient for integrating with web-based services, dashboards and microservices that expect RESTful APIs. If your team uses web stacks and wants lightweight JSON, RESTCONF reduces friction. If you must guarantee that a set of edits is applied together or you rely on commit/rollback cycles, NETCONF's candidate and commit model is safer. Performance and vendor support can also influence your choice; some platforms offer both and you may choose based on available modules and tools. A common misconception is that RESTCONF is always simpler; while it has web-friendly patterns, it still depends on correct YANG paths and does not inherently provide the same transactional guarantees. The practical rule: prefer NETCONF for complex, stateful configuration sequences that must be atomic; prefer RESTCONF for web integrations where idempotent operations and JSON are more practical.

screens.title: Common challenges and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Working with device APIs has recurring challenges you can overcome with disciplined practices. First, namespaces and paths: always verify the module prefix and exact path in YANG before sending a request. Mistaken namespaces are a leading cause of failed or ignored updates. Second, authentication and authorization: prefer certificates or token-based methods in production rather than basic auth and insecure flags; ensure the account you use has least-privilege needed for the task. Third, idempotency and transactional behavior: design operations so repeated calls do not produce unintended side effects; use NETCONF commits for atomic multi-step changes and RESTCONF idempotent methods like PUT where appropriate. Fourth, testing and rollback: always test in a lab environment, use read-back verification, and prepare rollback or discard procedures. Fifth, monitor and log responses: inspect status codes, rpc-reply details and error messages to guide remediation. A common misconception is that automation prevents human error; poorly constructed A P I calls can cause larger impact faster. The practical takeaway is to combine YANG literacy with a disciplined workflow: inspect, test, apply, verify, and have a rollback plan. fullNarratorScript:
In modern networking we move from typing commands to telling devices what state we want. This lesson explains the two cooperating pieces that make programmatic networking reliable: data models and APIs. A data model, specifically YANG, is the schema or blueprint that describes what configuration and state look like. An A P I like NETCONF or RESTCONF is the channel we use to read and change that data. You will learn why a common model matters, how NETCONF uses XML and RPCs over a secure transport with transactional operations, and how RESTCONF maps YANG to familiar HTTP methods and JSON payloads. We include practical examples you can run with curl and show the precise structure you must use so your scripts are robust across vendors and device versions. By the end you'll understand not only the vocabulary but how to choose the right tool for tasks, how to avoid common mistakes like wrong namespaces or inadequate privileges, and how to test safely in a lab before touching production devices. Imagine YANG as the blueprint of a house: it defines rooms, wiring and constraints. The APIs are your construction crew — one follows rigid contracts and transactions, the other speaks web-native HTTP. Which crew you pick depends on the work and risk: we'll make that decision easier.

These objectives target practical skills you need for safe, repeatable network automation. First, you'll explain why data models like YANG are necessary: they define the shape, types and constraints of configuration so automation tools interpret device data consistently. Second, you'll differentiate NETCONF and RESTCONF by their transport, encoding and operational model so you can choose the right A P I for a task. Third, you'll describe NETCONF and RESTCONF operations in detail, including NETCONF RPCs and RESTCONF HTTP methods, and how datastores and namespaces affect calls. Fourth, you'll demonstrate basic interactions using curl or a Python requests example to retrieve or change a hostname, showing exactly how to format requests and what to expect from the device. Each objective includes examples and a verification milestone so you can test competency in a lab. Achieving these objectives will let you automate deterministic changes, recover from mistakes, and integrate device APIs into higher-level automation tools. A frequent misconception is that APIs remove the need to understand the device model; in fact, model literacy is essential for correct paths, namespaces, and safe changes. We'll emphasize verification, minimal privileges and lab testing throughout.

These practice targets guide your lab work and assessments. First, identify the correct YANG path and namespace for a configuration element and explain how the model constrains valid values. For example, find the YANG path for an interface address or hostname and note required children. Second, map NETCONF RPCs to the state change you want: when to use edit-config and commit, when to lock a datastore, and why get-config differs from get. Third, write and run curl commands that authenticate to a RESTCONF endpoint, request JSON responses, and interpret the output. Fourth, adopt safety practices: use lab devices, minimize privileges, prefer idempotent HTTP methods, and confirm changes with a read-back. Each objective pairs a small verification: a GET that shows expected JSON, an edit that succeeds or rolls back, and a short explanation of the chosen path. These targets reduce accidental outages by making your automation predictable and verifiable before deployment. Remember, tools help, but model literacy and careful testing make automation safe.

Start with a precise distinction: a data model defines what data looks like and what rules apply; an A P I defines how you ask for or change that data. YANG is a data modeling language that describes configuration nodes, types, constraints and relationships. It specifies that an interface object, for example, includes fields such as description, IP address and operational status. Without such a model, a script might try different field names depending on the device, which breaks automation. APIs are the transport and syntax you use to interact with those modeled elements. NETCONF provides an XML-based RPC mechanism over a secure transport, with built-in operations like get, get-config, edit-config, commit and lock. RESTCONF exposes YANG-modeled data as HTTP resources, letting you use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with JSON or XML payloads. A useful analogy: YANG is an architectural blueprint, and NETCONF or RESTCONF are contractors who read that blueprint and execute changes. A common misconception is to assume that choosing an A P I removes the need to understand the model; in reality, correct A P I usage depends on knowing the exact YANG paths and namespaces. Practically, this means before running automation you must inspect the device's YANG modules, confirm namespaces and test read operations. The takeaway is simple: learn the model, then use the A P I. Which leads to safer, repeatable automation.

YANG is a language for expressing the schema of configuration and operational data on network devices. It defines containers, lists, leaf nodes, types and constraints so every element has a clear meaning. For example, a YANG model can require that an interface leaf supports an IP address with a specific pattern, or that a hostname leaf is a string under the native container. These definitions help automation by making values predictable and validating inputs before they're applied. A useful practice is to inspect the device's published YANG modules to find the correct namespace and hierarchical path; this step avoids the common error of referencing the wrong model or prefix. YANG also defines RPCs and notifications for device-specific operations and events, so you can standardize not only static configuration but also actions and alerts. A common misconception is that YANG is only for vendors; in reality it is an industry standard, and many vendors publish models for features across IOS XE and NX-OS. Practically, reading a YANG model is like reading a schema: it tells you what fields exist, which are mandatory, and the correct types. That knowledge is essential before crafting NETCONF XML or RESTCONF JSON payloads. Ask yourself: before you automate, have you opened the model and confirmed the exact path and namespace you will use?

NETCONF is an XML-based management protocol designed for network configuration. It operates over a secure transport, typically SSH, and uses remote procedure calls to request actions. Core operations include get to retrieve running configuration and state, get-config to fetch a specific datastore like running or startup, edit-config to propose changes to a target datastore, and commit to apply candidate changes to running. NETCONF supports a candidate datastore model where you stage changes and then commit them atomically, which reduces the risk of partial updates. Lock and unlock are important when concurrent actors may modify the same datastore; you lock to prevent others from changing it during your session. NETCONF replies are XML-encoded and include detailed status information. A concrete example: you assemble an XML edit-config payload that includes the native hostname element from the device's YANG module, send the RPC, then inspect the rpc-reply for success. A common misconception is that NETCONF is only for reads; in fact it was built specifically to make reliable configuration changes with transactional guarantees. The practical takeaway is to use NETCONF when you need atomic edits and explicit locking, especially in multi-user or multi-tool environments where consistency matters most.

Let's walk through a concrete NETCONF RPC payload used to set a hostname. NETCONF uses XML-encoded RPCs that include namespaces to identify the YANG module holding the target element. In this pattern you send an edit-config RPC that targets the running datastore and contains a config element with the module-qualified native container and the hostname leaf. The device responds with an rpc-reply indicating success or failure. Key details to note are the message-id for tracking, the base NETCONF namespace, and the module namespace for the specific element. A common mistake is omitting the module namespace or using an incorrect prefix; that causes the device to ignore the element or return an error. After sending the RPC, always inspect rpc-reply for ok or error details and consider using lock and commit when multiple processes might modify the datastore. The takeaway: constructing XML with the correct namespaces and using NETCONF's transactional semantics gives predictable, atomic configuration changes. Practice by comparing the payload to the device's YANG module so you confirm exact element names and structure. NETCONF example: XML edit-config means xml must include the correct netconf and module namespaces; missing or wrong namespaces lead to ignored or rejected edits.. In practical terms, a runnable xml rpc to set a hostname. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NETCONF includes mechanisms to make configuration changes safe and consistent. The typical workflow uses a candidate datastore: the client sends edits to the candidate, validates them, and then issues a commit to apply all changes to the running datastore in one atomic operation. If validation fails or an error occurs, you can discard the candidate, preventing partial updates. Lock and unlock protect a datastore from concurrent changes by other clients; use them when multiple automation tools or engineers might modify the same area. This transactional model prevents race conditions that occur when two processes try to update the same interface or route at the same time. A practical example: lock the running datastore, send a series of edit-config RPCs to update interface descriptions and IP addresses, validate the candidate, then commit. If any step fails, call discard-changes or unlock and investigate. A common misconception is that commits are instantaneous and risk-free; commits can fail due to validation, resource limits, or vendor-specific constraints, so always check rpc-reply details and plan rollback procedures. The key takeaway: use candidate + commit and lock/unlock to ensure predictable, all-or-nothing configuration changes under NETCONF.

RESTCONF is an HTTP-based protocol that maps YANG-modeled data to RESTful resources. It typically operates over HTTPS and uses JSON or XML payloads. The mapping is straightforward: YANG containers and lists become hierarchical URIs, and standard HTTP methods correspond to operations on those resources. Use GET to retrieve configuration or operational data, POST to create new entries, PUT to replace a resource, PATCH to partially update, and DELETE to remove a resource. RESTCONF commonly returns JSON when you request application/yang-data+json. Because RESTCONF uses familiar web concepts, it is often easier for web developers and microservices to integrate with network devices. A common misconception is that RESTCONF is always less reliable than NETCONF; while it is more web-native and lightweight, RESTCONF still relies on YANG for structure and can be used safely if you understand idempotency semantics of methods like PUT and PATCH. Use RESTCONF when you prefer HTTP ecosystems, integration with web tooling, or lightweight JSON payloads. For transactional guarantees, consider whether your workflow requires NETCONF's explicit commit semantics, because RESTCONF typically relies on HTTP's idempotency rather than multi-step commits.
